opus-5.5.text:
So the way we think about it is that you're not really optimizing for training cost alone. You're optimizing for the total cost of the model over its lifetime. If you train a model once and then serve it to millions of users, inference quickly becomes the dominant cost. That changes how you should allocate compute.

The scaling laws people often refer to, the Chinchilla-style laws, tell you how to get the best model for a fixed training budget. But that isn't the question a business should ask. The real question is: what's the best model I can serve at a given price point, with a given latency? If you take that view, it makes sense to train smaller models for much longer, on many more tokens than the "compute-optimal" recipe suggests. You pay more upfront in training, but you get a model that's cheaper and faster to run, and that compounds every time someone calls it.

That's been a big part of our approach from the start. We focused on making models that are very efficient for their size, models developers can actually deploy, sometimes on their own infrastructure, without needing a huge cluster for every request. Compression and efficiency are central to the value we deliver, not just nice side properties.

There's also an architectural angle. Sparse approaches like mixture of experts let you have a lot of parameters, so a lot of capacity and knowledge, while activating only a fraction of them per token. So you decouple the model's knowledge from what it costs to serve. That's another lever for getting the inference economics right.

And then there's a portfolio question. Not every use case needs the largest model. Many enterprise workloads, like classification, extraction, routing, or summarization, run perfectly well on smaller, specialized models, and those are where the volume is. So you want a family of models: some frontier-level models for the hardest reasoning tasks, and very efficient smaller ones for high-throughput work. Customers can pick the right trade-off, and that's what makes the business sustainable. You aren't burning money serving a giant model for a task a small one handles just as well.

So in short, think about the lifetime cost of the model, invest more in training to make inference cheap, and give people the right size of model for the job.

r001.rationale: The response argues that inference cost matters over a model’s lifetime, but does not explain that inference cost is not a priority when building solely to assess achievable performance.

r002.rationale: It recommends weighing upfront training against serving costs for a viable business, but does not state that the appropriate balance depends on the business model.

r003.rationale: It describes efficient models that developers can deploy and lists several use cases, but does not clearly identify cheap inference as what enables widespread LLM use across applications.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way we think about it is that training cost is something you pay once, and inference cost is something you pay every time someone uses the model. So if you actually have users, inference is where the economics live. That changes how you design the model from the start.

What a lot of people got wrong in the early days, and I include the scaling-law papers here, is that they optimized for training compute. Chinchilla tells you the optimal number of tokens per parameter if you only care about the cost of training. But that's not the problem you have as a business. The problem you have is: for a given quality level, what's the cheapest model to serve? And the answer is almost always a smaller model trained on far more tokens than Chinchilla would suggest. You overspend on training so that you underspend on inference, and if the model is used enough, that pays for itself very quickly.

That's essentially the bet we made with the first 7B model. We trained it much longer than was "optimal" in the training-compute sense, and the result was something that was cheap to run on a single GPU, or even on a laptop, and still competitive with models two or three times its size. Then with the mixture-of-experts work, you get another lever: you can have a lot of parameters, so a lot of capacity, but only activate a fraction of them per token. So your inference cost looks like a small dense model while the quality looks like a much bigger one. Those architectural choices are really inference decisions.

There's also the memory side, which people underestimate. Inference is often bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, so things like grouped-query attention and sliding-window attention matter because they shrink the KV cache. That's not about FLOPs, it's about being able to batch more requests on the same hardware, which directly lowers your cost per token.

And then the last point is that the training cost is itself a lever on the business, because if you're efficient at training, you can iterate faster, and iteration speed is most of what determines model quality over a year. So I'd say we don't really think of it as a trade-off between the two. We think of training as an investment, and we size that investment based on how much inference we expect the model to generate. If you get that calculation right, the model pays for itself. If you get it wrong, you've built something very expensive that nobody can afford to run.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training-compute optimization with business-serving costs, but does not say inference cost is unimportant when assessing achievable performance alone.

r002.rationale: It says the training investment should be sized according to expected inference usage, making the cost balance depend on the business’s anticipated use of the model.

r003.rationale: It describes models that are cheap to run on limited hardware, but does not connect cheap inference to widespread LLM use across applications.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at the full lifetime of the model. Training is an upfront investment, whereas inference is a cost you incur every time someone uses it. So if you expect a model to serve a lot of traffic, it can make sense to spend more on training to get the same quality from a smaller model. You pay more once, but then you save on every request, and you improve latency as well.

The question is really: what capability does the customer need, and how efficiently can you deliver it? For many applications, you don’t need the most capable model for every query. You need a model that does a particular job reliably, at the right price. So model size, training effort, and how you serve the model all have to be considered together.

And that balance depends on usage. If you train something very expensive and nobody uses it, you haven’t made a good investment. If it gets used at enormous scale, then investing more upfront to reduce the inference cost can be very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response treats inference as an ongoing cost that matters and does not say it can be ignored when building a model solely to assess achievable performance.

r002.rationale: It says the balance depends on usage, expected traffic, and the customer’s needs, and describes how those factors affect the training-versus-inference tradeoff.

r003.rationale: It discusses reducing per-request cost and serving traffic at scale, but does not identify cheap inference as enabling widespread LLM use across applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to optimize the two together. Training is a large upfront investment, but inference is a cost you pay every time someone uses the model. So if you expect a model to serve a lot of traffic, spending more during training to make it smaller and more efficient can be a very good trade.

The objective isn’t simply to get the best benchmark score. It’s to reach the quality a customer needs at a cost and latency that make the application useful. For some tasks, you need a very capable model. For many others, a smaller model, perhaps adapted to the task, is sufficient and much more economical.

So the business question is: how much useful work can you deliver for a given amount of compute? You have to think about that from the beginning, because a model that is impressive but too expensive to serve is difficult to build a business around.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference cost as a recurring expense and says it matters for viability; it does not say inference cost is unimportant when building a model solely to assess achievable performance.

r002.rationale: It describes a trade-off based on expected traffic and customer needs, but does not state that the relative weighting of inference and training costs depends on the business model.

r003.rationale: It says efficient models can make applications more economical, but does not identify cheap inference as enabling widespread LLM use across applications.
